solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Wow! Female in New Jersey, say, making bloomer

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another is placed between its letters, here between two parts

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise
N is the standard abbreviation for new
F is the abbreviation for female
a Jersey is a breed of cow, and a cow is something that lows

explanation.surface: Someone is amazed at a woman in the American state of New Jersey who turns out to be a late developer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Jersey' looks like the US state, but it splits into N and a Jersey cow, which is a 'lower' because it lows; the female sits between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer here is simply a thing that blooms, and this blue wildflower of cornfields does exactly that.

clue.text: It's played in place people are confined with ball

parts.note: a prison cell is where inmates are locked up
O is round, like a ball

explanation.surface: A game is being played inside a prison, with a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a sport in a jail yard; the 'it' that is played is an instrument, not a game.
explanation.definitionFit: A musician plays this stringed instrument, so a cryptic description of it is something that gets played.

clue.text: Criticise and maybe drone on loudly, getting meal

parts.note: to roast someone is to criticise them harshly
a drone is a male bee, one example of a bee
F (forte) is the musical direction for loud

explanation.surface: Someone who complains and drones on at volume is rewarded with dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drone on' reads as a phrasal verb meaning talk boringly, but the drone is a noun, a male bee, and 'maybe' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the traditional British Sunday joint, a cooked dish served as the main course of a dinner.

clue.text: Oddly, finer dress stores maintain no returns policy

indicators.note: to store is to keep something inside, so one string holds another within it
done oddly means done in a strange, irregular way, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ten letters to rearrange
to maintain something is to keep it

explanation.surface: A smart clothes shop has a strict policy of no refunds on its finer dresses.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten rearranged letters split into two parts with the verb for maintain between them; 'stores' looks like shops but is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The playground saying claims whoever picks something up may keep it, so nothing found is ever given back to its owner.

clue.text: Monstrous error when defending dissolute heirs

parts.note: OG is an own goal, the classic football blunder by a defender

indicators.note: dissolute means loose and disorderly in conduct, so these letters fall into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone makes a terrible mistake in standing up for a pair of debauched heirs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when defending' seems to say the error contains something, but the whole phrase is one idea: an own goal, the mistake a defender makes in football.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a fairytale monster, so behaving like one is to be monstrous in manner or appearance.

clue.text: Even heartless crimes stopped by good standards

indicators.note: without a heart means the middle is cut out and only the ends survive

parts.note: the word with its middle two letters removed

indicators.note: something stopped by a plug has that plug sitting inside its opening

parts.note: sins are wrongdoings
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Even pitiless crimes are halted by good moral standards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' looks like an adverb for emphasis but is the word to be gutted; 'standards' looks moral but means flags.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a flag carried as an emblem, and an ensign is a flag flown especially at sea.

clue.text: Member has pounds, investing one million

indicators.note: to invest is literally to clothe or wrap, so one part is placed inside another

parts.note: lb is the abbreviation for pounds weight
I is the Roman numeral for one
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: A club member has money and is putting it into a million-pound scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'investing' reads as finance but means wrapping around, a sense from investing someone with robes.
explanation.definitionFit: An arm or leg is a member of the body in the old anatomical sense of a jointed part.

clue.text: Periodically miss old cover of Adam Faith

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the even-placed letters of these words

indicators.note: the cover is the outside layer, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the name

explanation.surface: Someone sometimes misses an old cover version of a song by Adam Faith, the 1960s British pop singer.
explanation.walkthrough: Adam Faith was a British pop star, so 'cover' sounds like a cover version; the definition is the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: This is one of the world's major monotheistic religions, and a faith is a religious belief system.

clue.text: Ordered to imprison lousy red for not rising

indicators.note: a prisoner is held inside a cell, so one piece holds another

parts.note: to be bidden is to be told or ordered to do something

indicators.note: lousy means poor or bad, so these letters are in poor shape and must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A worthless communist is ordered to be jailed for failing to join an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'red' suggests a communist and 'not rising' a failed revolt, but the phrase simply means unable to get up.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone confined to bed by illness or age cannot get up, so they are literally never out of bed.

clue.text: Selfish hoarder of alcohol those people put out after party

indicators.note: coming after something means following it, so the remaining pieces are placed behind it

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party
gin is one kind of alcoholic spirit
the pronoun for those people as object
to put someone out is to annoy or anger them

explanation.surface: A selfish guest hogs the drink and annoys everyone after the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out' looks like evicting the guests, but it is the verb meaning to annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: From Aesop, the dog lies in the hay it cannot eat to stop the ox having it; the idiom describes someone keeping what they cannot use.

clue.text: Money-spinner goes on line in The Apprentice

indicators.note: in an across clue, going on something means being placed after it

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for line
a nice little earner is something that brings in money

explanation.surface: A money-making contestant is on the line on The Apprentice, the business reality TV show.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitalised 'The Apprentice' points at the TV show, but only the noun is the definition, the article belonging to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An apprentice is someone learning a trade, so a trainee or novice still mastering skills.

clue.text: Showed anger in society, like brothers in the hood?

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for society
monks and friars, called brothers, wear hooded robes known as cowls

explanation.surface: Someone got angry at the way gang members behave in a rough neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brothers in the hood' sounds like street slang for gang members; the brothers are monks and the hood is a real hood, a cowl.
explanation.definitionFit: To frown with displeasure is a facial expression of anger, so this is showing annoyance on the face.

clue.text: Swallowing umpteenth tablet, unsettled in flight

indicators.note: whatever is swallowed ends up inside, so one piece engulfs others

parts.note: an unsettled bill is one still owing
nth means the latest in an indefinitely long series
E is slang for an ecstasy tablet

explanation.surface: A nervous flyer has swallowed yet another pill and is still uneasy on the plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unsettled' looks like an anagram signal or nervousness, but it means unpaid, as a debt is.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird that is flying is said to be on the wing, an idiom for being airborne.

clue.text: Most of this person's large feet

indicators.note: most rather than all means a little is missing from the end

parts.note: the setter speaking of themselves: this person is, so I am
big means large

explanation.surface: The setter admits to having big feet.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is', not a possessive; the last letter of the whole phrase is then dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: In verse, a foot is a unit of metre, and an iamb is one short then one long syllable; this is the Latin plural.

clue.text: Hardy female grasping right head adornment

indicators.note: to grasp is to hold tightly, so one piece is gripped inside another

parts.note: Tess of the d'Urbervilles is Thomas Hardy's best-known heroine
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A tough woman reaches for the correct hat or headdress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like an adjective meaning tough; with its capital it is the novelist Thomas Hardy.
explanation.definitionFit: A long lock of hair grows from the head and decorates it, so it is fairly called an adornment.

clue.text: Cheers small canine, pointer according to Spooner

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds trade places

parts.note: a toy poodle is a small dog; its opening P trades with the T of the next word
the tip is the pointed end of something; its opening T trades with the P before it

explanation.surface: Someone toasts a little dog and a pointer, a gun dog breed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pointer' looks like another dog breed, but it means a tip. Swap the opening sounds of the dog and the tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheers is a casual British way of saying goodbye, and this dated jolly phrase is another farewell.

clue.text: Wasn't sure English model despised clothes

indicators.note: to clothe someone is to wrap them, so one piece is dressed around another

parts.note: to despise is to hate
E is the abbreviation for English
to model for an artist is to sit

explanation.surface: Someone dithered about whether an English fashion model disliked the outfits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothes' reads as a noun, garments, but it is the verb: the outer word dresses the inner pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To pause in uncertainty before acting is to be unsure, so the past tense matches being undecided.

clue.text: Least tasteful twit dares to get a make-over

indicators.note: a make-over remodels a look completely, so these letters are restyled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The silliest fool, the one with the worst taste, finally ventures to have a makeover.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the start, and the surface's tasteless fool is exactly who needs a makeover.
explanation.definitionFit: Tawdry means cheap and showy, so the superlative describes whatever is gaudiest and lowest in taste.

clue.text: Switch positions round areas for sailing in quiet time

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so the outer pair surround the middle

parts.note: a light switch has two settings, off and on
seas are where ships sail

explanation.surface: Crew swap places on board while sailing during a calm spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Switch positions' sounds like changing places; it means the two settings of a switch, which split to go either side.
explanation.definitionFit: Resorts and businesses have a slack period when few visitors come, the least busy part of the year.

clue.text: Poet one introduced to Eliot, initially, around spring

indicators.note: turning around faces the other way, so the letters run backwards
introducing something to a place puts it in there, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: the poet T. S. Eliot's initials
I is the Roman numeral for one
a spring is a natural source of water, a well

explanation.surface: One poet is introduced to T. S. Eliot early in his career, around springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' seems to mean the first letter of Eliot, but it means his initials, T and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Edith Sitwell was an English modernist poet, one of the three literary Sitwell siblings.

clue.text: Stick up banks in Lancashire, which is interesting

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a baton is a stick, as used by a conductor or police officer

indicators.note: the banks of a river are its edges, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the county name

explanation.surface: Armed robbers hold up banks in Lancashire, an English county, which makes for an interesting story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick up banks' reads as an armed robbery; it is a stick turned upside down and the edges of a county name.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worth noting is remarkable or striking, so it deserves attention and holds interest.

clue.text: King of Northumbria emerged drained by victory

indicators.note: a drained container has its contents emptied out, so only the outside letters are left

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
a win is a victory

explanation.surface: An ancient king came out of battle exhausted but victorious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drained' suggests the king was exhausted, but it empties the word before it of its middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Edwin was the seventh-century Anglo-Saxon ruler of Northumbria, the first of its kings to become Christian.

clue.text: Place this person left, backing out of it?

indicators.note: backing means moving in the rearward direction, so the string runs from end to start

parts.note: to place something is to put it
the setter referring to themselves
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone describes a place they once left, retreating from it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of it' looks like leaving the place, but it is slang for drunk; the question mark flags that playful sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Being lit up is an informal way of saying intoxicated, and someone out of it is drunk or stoned.

clue.text: Fish like sashimi, say, in wrapping of tinfoil

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it
a wrapping is the outer layer, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
sashimi is uncooked fish, an example of raw food

explanation.surface: Fish such as sashimi is wrapped in kitchen foil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' looks like a noun, the sashimi itself, but it is the verb for fishing with a net.
explanation.definitionFit: To trawl is to fish by dragging a large net behind a boat.

clue.text: Four-letter word from guy probing complex matter

indicators.note: a probe pushes into something, so one piece is inserted into another
complex means intricate and tangled, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange
to guy someone is to tease or rag them

explanation.surface: A man swears while looking into a complicated problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Four-letter word' suggests a swear word and 'guy' a man; the guy is the verb meaning to mock.
explanation.definitionFit: A tetragram is a word of four letters, from Greek for four and letter.

clue.text: Musician's very beastly utterance about officer

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: a moo is the sound a cow makes
Lt is the abbreviation for lieutenant

explanation.surface: A musician makes a very rude remark about an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very beastly' reads as an intensifier for nasty, but 'very' belongs with 'Musician's' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In musical directions the Italian word for much intensifies a tempo marking, as in molto allegro.

clue.text: Work to improve image and appearance that is plain

parts.note: PR, public relations, is work to polish a reputation
an air is a manner or appearance
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Image consultants try to improve someone whose looks are frankly plain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plain' looks like an adjective for an unremarkable appearance; it is the noun for flat grassland.
explanation.definitionFit: A prairie is a vast treeless grassland of North America, the classic example of a plain.

clue.text: E.g. pine to put on odd bits of bling that's unimpressive

indicators.note: in an across clue, putting one thing on another places it after
odd here means odd-numbered, so the first, third and fifth letters are kept

parts.note: the odd-placed letters of the word
deal is softwood timber such as pine

explanation.surface: Someone longs to wear showy jewellery that is in fact rather paltry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pine' looks like a verb, to yearn; it is the tree, an example of deal wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Said sarcastically, the phrase dismisses something as no great matter, so it is a retort meaning so what.

clue.text: Huge amount of money for a swanky residence

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a large imposing house

explanation.surface: A fortune is paid for a posh mansion.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one transaction, but the two halves are separate meanings of the same short word.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally the word means a great sum of money, and also a large grand building such as a country house.

clue.text: Caught in squall, egret toppled pretty quickly

indicators.note: something caught in the following words is held inside them, sitting within the letters

parts.note: the letters run on across these words

explanation.surface: A wading bird caught in a storm is knocked over very fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'toppled' hints at reversal, but the letters read forwards, ignoring the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: In music this tempo marking means fairly brisk, a little slower than allegro, so moderately fast.
